This is a classic motte-and-bailey fallacy. See e.g. here. This is where there are two versions of a claim that sound very similar, and one defends one version when one is pressed on it, but one uses a stronger version for other purposes. In this case, you are making a specific claim that some Democrats are being selfish where there's a clear implication that they are being selfish in an atypical fashion, but the fall-back defendable version of the claim is only in the absolutely trivial sense that all motivations are selfish since they follow one's own desires even if those desires are to help others or the like.

This sort of fallacy is common throughout the political spectrum. One sees it for example on some parts of the left when people use privilege to mean something like "I don't have to listen to you anything you say if you are from a certain group" but when they need to defend the claim they intend use privilege to mean something like "some aspects of society systematically make things easier for some people and the people who it is easier for may not notice this." See for example the last link I gave. In this situation it is worth noting that one also sees nearly identical behavior with MRAs, where there are defensible versions of central claims that they retreat to, but then in other contexts act like the broad versions are what apply.
